papers.title: Price-Volume Correlations Are Always Zero
papers.abstract: We argue that the use of the empirical time series of values, volumes, and prices of consecutive trades made during the averaging interval to calculate the price-volume correlation in a way that follows the definition of correlation always gives zero correlation. We show that the usual expression for the empirical calculation of the correlation misleads the researchers and doesn't fulfill the definition of price-volume correlation. The mistake has its origin in the dependence of volume weighted average price on the mean values and volumes of trades during the averaging interval but not on time series of prices only. The true sense of the declared positive or negative results of the empirical calculations of price-volume correlations made by numerous researchers in reality is determined by the difference between the volume weighted average price and its limiting expression of average price, which is correct only when all volumes of consecutive trades are constant, and multiplication of this difference by the mean trade volume. To empirically determine the statistical dependence between time series of prices and trade volumes, one should calculate the correlations between prices and squares of trade volumes or correlations between squares of prices and squares of volumes. We derive the expressions for empirical calculations of these correlations.

papers.title: The End-of-Day Reversal After 2019: A Pre-Registered Test on S&P 500 Stocks Excluding Heavily Traded Names
papers.abstract: Baltussen, Da and Soebhag (2025) document an end-of-day reversal in U.S. stocks through December 2019: intraday losers outperform intraday winners over the last half hour of trading. We test it on later data, on point-in-time S&P 500 members excluding about 80 heavily traded stocks we had examined in earlier, unpublished work. Under a private pre-registration, the 2016-2019 data had to reproduce the published sign before any statistic linking the sort to the outcome was computed on later primary-sample data. Measured to the last trade before the closing auction, the dollar-volume-weighted reversal is 3.13 bps per day (t = 7.5) in 2016-2019 and 3.05 bps (t = 3.0) in 2023-2026, with a one-sided 95% bound on the decline of 61%. The result depends on the window: the reversal is indistinguishable from zero in 2020-2022, 2023 carries much of the later estimate, and from 2020 onward it is 1.69 bps (t = 2.3), with a bound of 91%. A proxy sample, added after the run, gives 2.81 and 3.86 bps. On the full index the reversal falls from 3.40 to 0.74 bps (t of the change -1.83, short of the registered bar of -3); descriptive comparisons concentrate this weakness in the very largest stocks. No pre-registered mechanism test passes.

papers.title: Isotonic Quantile Regression Averaging for uncertainty quantification of electricity price forecasts
papers.abstract: Quantifying the uncertainty of forecasting models is essential to assess and mitigate the risks associated with data-driven decisions, especially in volatile domains such as electricity markets. In this paper, we propose a computationally efficient isotonic variant of Quantile Regression Averaging (QRA), called Isotonic Quantile Regression Averaging (iQRA), for generating probabilistic forecasts from ensembles of point forecasts. Building on QRA, we introduce stochastic order constraints as a hyperparameter-free regularization mechanism that reduces computational complexity while maintaining competitive forecast accuracy. We further demonstrate that the same isotonic regularization principle can be applied to the smoothed estimator of QRA. In an extensive forecasting study of two European day-ahead electricity markets, we show that iQRA and its smoothed variant consistently rank among the top state-of-the-art postprocessing methods in terms of reliability and sharpness. It produces well-calibrated prediction intervals, with smoothed iQRA providing superior reliability even when compared against coverage-oriented conformal prediction. We further introduce a battery arbitrage evaluation, showing that the leading probabilistic methods achieve the highest profit per trade and that probabilistic risk control improves the economic value of trading decisions. Isotonic regularization offers a scalable hyperparameter-free variable selection for linear quantile regression, making iQRA attractive for practical decision-support systems in energy markets.

papers.title: Who Are a Firm's Economic Peers? Mapping a Latent Information Field with Language Models
papers.abstract: Identifying a firm's economic peers matters for benchmarking, risk measurement, and understanding return dependence, yet a diversified firm may have no single natural peer. We use language-model representations of corporate news to identify the combination of firms that jointly represents each firm's information environment. Each firm is represented by a distribution of article embeddings, and target-anchored Wasserstein barycentric reconstruction produces a directed map of economic-peer weights. We use this map as the interaction structure in a spatial factor model and ask whether return dependence follows peer relations measured from news without using returns. We construct peer weights from 2018-2022 news for 100 large-cap US traded firms and evaluate their financial relevance in subsequent returns. Relative to a matched model with the Fama-French five factors and momentum, the information field firms' unexpected returns move together after common factor exposures are accounted for. Joint reconstruction contributes substantially more than pairwise Wasserstein proximity or equal weighting of the selected peers, while centroid reconstruction retains most of the gain. Explicit news co-mentions provide complementary information. Language models thus make the interaction structure in spatial asset pricing an object of measurement: economically interpretable peer relations can be constructed from text before their financial relevance is assessed in returns.

papers.title: Portfolio Risk Bounds without Cross-Asset Return Covariances: Distributional Fields from Language-Model Representations
papers.abstract: Portfolio risk assessment ordinarily relies on reliable estimates of cross-asset return covariances, which are difficult to obtain in short, high-dimensional panels. We show that firm-level distribution-valued characteristics can instead provide one-sided certificates of portfolio risk. Under maintained links from characteristics to systematic exposures and from exposures to returns, multi-firm Wasserstein-2 dispersion yields a sharp upper bound on systematic portfolio variance and a corresponding bound for standardized returns. A weighted pairwise relaxation produces an objective that is convex under a checkable condition and requires marginal volatility scales but no cross-asset return covariances. With zero firm-specific slack, the common-map scale changes the certified variance reduction but not the normalized allocation, which depends only on observed information geometry. In a 100-firm panel from 2018-2022, only 0.09%-0.46% of portfolios across four prespecified capped reference populations have in-sample variance no greater than an allocation constructed from Qwen3-Embedding-8B news representations; the corresponding share for equal risk weighting is 28.3%-34.7%. The lower in-sample variance ranking relative to equal risk also appears across the reported frozen language-model representations. The framework therefore converts distribution-valued firm information into a coherent risk bound and an implementable allocation rule constructed without cross-asset return covariances.
